theory1.instructions: Answer all 45 questions. Each question has one best answer: choose it. Each question is worth 1 mark. Time allowed: 2 hours 30 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

questions.stem: A ministry must explain a complex new pension rule to its staff, the staff unions and retired officers. What should the communications lead do first?
options: Write one detailed circular and send it to every group
Post the full rule on the website and wait for questions
Analyse each audience's needs, concerns and knowledge
Book the largest hall and invite every group at once

questions.stem: On a power-interest grid, how should an agency usually treat a group with high power and high interest in a policy?
options: Involve it closely and consult it often
Keep it informed with a yearly newsletter
Watch it from a distance, with little contact
Leave it out until the policy is final

questions.stem: A citizens' association is very interested in a road project but has little formal power over it. How should the agency communicate with the association?
options: Leave it out until the project is complete
Contact it only if it begins a public protest
Send it the technical drawings without comment
Keep it well informed and listen to its views

questions.stem: A municipal corporation officer explains a new garbage collection schedule at a community meeting, and many residents look confused. Which barrier is most likely?
options: The residents have no interest in garbage collection
Technical terms and too much detail at once
The meeting room was lit far too brightly
The officer spoke for less than ten minutes

questions.stem: Which sentence best explains a policy change to members of the public?
options: Pursuant to the revised framework, eligibility criteria are amended.
Eligibility is henceforth contingent upon residency status.
The criteria for qualifying have undergone modification.
From 1 May, you must have lived here for a year to qualify.

questions.stem: A government agency will close one of its regional offices. Who should usually hear the news first?
options: The staff of that office, in person
The media, through a press release
The public, through a notice on the website
Other agencies, at their next joint meeting

questions.stem: A unit head must explain to her team a restructure that changes several jobs. Which approach is best?
options: A short email to everyone with the new chart attached
A notice on the board listing the new job titles
A team meeting, then one-to-one talks and a summary
Waiting for the rumours to settle before saying anything

questions.stem: A public agency's consultation documents will be read by some people with visual impairments. What should it provide?
options: Documents in a smaller font to save paper
Large print and screen-reader versions
Printed copies at the head office only
Colour-coded charts with no words at all

questions.stem: A project team includes officers from several Caribbean countries and an adviser from Japan. How should the team leader communicate in meetings?
options: Use plenty of local sayings to help everyone bond
Speak faster so that the meetings finish sooner
Assume that everyone reads meaning in the same way
Check understanding and avoid slang and idioms

questions.stem: An angry taxpayer complains at a tax office counter. Which reply shows active listening?
options: 'So the main problem is you were sent away twice?'
'Please calm down, or I will have to call security.'
'I am sorry, sir, that is not my department at all.'
'Everyone has to wait here; you are no different.'

questions.stem: Which action best calms a heated conversation with an upset service user?
options: Raise your voice so that you can be heard clearly
Tell the person that their feelings are mistaken
Stay calm, listen and acknowledge the concern
Walk away until the person has stopped shouting

questions.stem: During a meeting at a public office, a member of the public becomes threatening. What should the officer do?
options: Argue back firmly to show who is in charge
Follow the safety procedure and get help
Lock the door so that the person cannot leave
Promise whatever the person is demanding

questions.stem: An officer must tell a contractor that its application for registration has been refused. What is the best approach?
options: Send a one-line email that gives no reasons
Avoid contact and let the contractor find out
Say a colleague's mistake caused the refusal
Explain the reasons clearly and the next steps

questions.stem: Two senior officers in a unit disagree openly in meetings, and staff are taking sides. What should the manager do first?
options: Meet each one privately to hear their concerns
Tell the whole team which officer is right
Move one of the officers to another unit at once
Ignore it as a normal part of office life

questions.stem: Two units both want the only meeting room every Monday morning. On talking, one needs privacy for interviews and the other needs a projector. What should the facilitator do?
options: Toss a coin to decide who gets the room
Give the room to the more senior unit head
Look for options that meet both real needs
Stop both units from using the room at all

questions.stem: At the start of a stakeholder workshop, what should the facilitator do?
options: Begin with the most heated issue on the list
Agree the purpose, agenda and ground rules
Ask the senior people to speak for everyone
Hand out the final decision to be signed

questions.stem: One participant dominates a consultation meeting while others stay silent. What should the facilitator do?
options: Let him carry on, as he clearly knows the most
Close the meeting early to avoid any tension
Ask the silent participants to leave the room
Thank him and invite the others' views in turn

questions.stem: A participant raises an important issue that is outside the workshop's agenda. What should the facilitator do?
options: Note it on a list for later follow-up
Spend the rest of the session on it
Tell the participant that it does not matter
Ask the participant to leave the workshop

questions.stem: A working group cannot agree on one option. Which method helps it reach a decision most fairly?
options: Let whoever speaks the longest make the decision
Leave the decision to the newest member
Rank the options against agreed criteria
Postpone the decision with no new date set

questions.stem: Why should the outcomes of a consultation meeting be written up and shared with the participants?
options: To prove that the facilitator was there
So all can check their views were recorded fairly
To replace the need for any decision at all
So that the notes can then be kept secret

questions.stem: An officer will represent her unit at an inter-agency meeting on flood response. What should she do beforehand?
options: Decide her own personal views and present them
Plan to say nothing until the others have spoken
Bring every file the unit has ever kept on floods
Agree the unit's position and limits with her manager

questions.stem: At an inter-agency meeting, another agency asks the officer to lend her unit's staff for a month. She has no authority to agree. What should she say?
options: She will take it back and reply by an agreed date
Yes, as agreeing will build good relations
No, as her unit is always far too busy
Nothing, in the hope that it is forgotten

questions.stem: Which structure best suits a briefing note for a Permanent Secretary who must decide an issue today?
options: Background and full history first, with the options at the end
A long account of every meeting held on the issue
Purpose, key facts, options and a recommendation
A list of questions for the reader to look into

questions.stem: A technical report on water quality must be shared with a citizens' association. What is the best approach?
options: Send the full technical report without any change
Write a plain-language summary and offer a briefing
Send only the charts and tables, with no words
Refuse, as the public would not understand it

questions.stem: Why should a public consultation paper state clearly what is still open to change?
options: To keep the consultation as short as it can be
To discourage people from sending responses
To show that the decision has already been made
So people know where their views can count

questions.stem: A director receives strong criticism from staff at a town hall meeting. How should she respond?
options: Thank them, ask questions and say what happens next
Defend every decision, point by point, at length
Close the meeting at once and leave the room
Ask who organised the complaints against her

questions.stem: In a video meeting with officers from several parishes, many cameras are off and few people speak. What can the chair do?
options: Carry on talking until the time is up
Insist that every camera is switched on
Use names, polls and chat to draw people in
End the call and email the slides instead

questions.stem: Different officers have given the public different answers about a new fee. What should the agency do?
options: Let each officer explain it in their own way
Agree key messages and brief front-line staff
Stop answering any questions about the fee
Publish a correction only if the media asks

questions.stem: A ministry's staff survey shows that many officers learn about changes from the media first. What should management do?
options: Ask the media to stop reporting the changes
Send all news by post to staff members' homes
Ban staff from reading the news while at work
Review its internal channels and their timing

questions.stem: Which question best helps an officer understand a complainant's situation?
options: 'Can you tell me what happened, from the start?'
'You did fill in the form properly, didn't you?'
'Was it on Tuesday or on Wednesday?'
'Why didn't you come to us much earlier?'

questions.stem: A junior officer has an important safety concern but is nervous about raising it with senior managers in a meeting. What should her manager do?
options: Tell her to wait until she is more senior
Raise it as his own idea to save some time
Give her a safe chance to raise it
Ask her to email the minister about it directly

questions.stem: Three agencies will run a joint service centre. What will most help them communicate well with each other?
options: Each agency keeping its own separate messages
Agreed contacts, channels and a joint plan
Using formal letters for every contact
Leaving the public to pass news between them

questions.stem: How can a health department find out whether its public campaign on dengue prevention was understood?
options: Count how many posters were printed
Ask the design agency whether it liked them
Assume it worked if nobody complains
Survey residents on what they know and do

questions.stem: Many clients of a social welfare office have low literacy. How should officers explain a new application process?
options: Talk it through, show the steps and check
Give each client a long printed guide to read
Refer every client to the agency's website
Tell them to bring a relative who can read

questions.stem: A Deaf applicant attends an interview at a public agency. What should the agency arrange?
options: Officers who speak loudly so he can lip-read
Written notes only, with no other support
A qualified sign language interpreter
A family member to interpret, to save cost

questions.stem: An officer must give bad news to a family who are visibly distressed. What should she do?
options: Give all the details quickly and move on
Speak gently, give key facts and allow time
Put it off without saying until when
Ask a junior colleague to tell them instead

questions.stem: An officer wants senior management to fund a new client feedback system. Which approach is most persuasive?
options: Repeat the request at every meeting she attends
Complain to colleagues about the lack of money
Send one long email that lists every problem
Present the evidence, costs, benefits and options

questions.stem: During a consultation, a resident shares private information about a neighbour. How should the officer handle it?
options: Leave it out of public notes and follow policy
Read it out so that everyone is informed
Include it in the published consultation report
Tell the neighbour about it straight away

questions.stem: A ministry plans a two-week public consultation on a major change during the Christmas season. Why is this a poor choice?
options: The law does not allow consultations in December
Every consultation must last exactly one month
Few people will have time to respond well
Staff are not allowed to work during holidays

questions.stem: When explaining a new property tax rule, how should the message to business owners differ from the message to elderly homeowners?
options: It should be the same, word for word, for both
Same facts, with examples and channels to suit each
Business owners should be given fewer of the facts
Elderly homeowners should not be told at all

questions.stem: How should a facilitator close a stakeholder workshop?
options: Leave as soon as the time runs out
Ask the most senior person to decide everything
Hand out a survey and go without comment
Sum up agreements, actions and next steps

questions.stem: Why is a face-to-face meeting often better than email for discussing a complex, contentious issue?
options: People can ask questions and see reactions
It leaves no record of what was said
It is always quicker than writing
Nobody is able to disagree in person

questions.stem: An officer has ten minutes to explain a planning decision at a public meeting. Which approach works best?
options: Read the whole legal decision aloud, word for word
Speak only about the history of the area
Give the key points, reasons and how to respond
Take questions only, with no explanation first

questions.stem: Residents ask for a promise that a closed clinic will reopen next month, but no decision has been made. What should the officer say?
options: Promise that it will reopen, to calm the meeting
What is known, what is not, and when they will hear
That the clinic will certainly never reopen
Nothing at all about the clinic's future

questions.stem: After leading a difficult consultation, how can an officer best improve her communication skills?
options: Avoid leading any consultations in future
Assume it went well because it ended on time
Ask only her close friends how she did
Reflect on feedback and plan what to change

theory2.instructions: Section A has 15 short answers (2 marks each). Section B has 10 essay questions (5 marks each): answer each in full sentences. Time allowed: 3 hours 35 minutes. Your answers are saved as you go.

shortAnswers.stem: What term names the grid that sorts stakeholders by how much power they have and how interested they are in an issue?
What one-word term names restating what a speaker has said in your own words, to check that you understood?
What one-word term names a group decision that every member can accept, even if it is not everyone's first choice?
What two-word term names the agreed rules for behaviour set at the start of a meeting or workshop?
What one-word term names a session in which people put forward as many ideas as possible without judging them?
What one-word term names reducing the tension in a heated exchange, for example by staying calm, listening and acknowledging feelings?
A speaker talks at about 130 words a minute. About how many words should she prepare for a 10-minute talk?
What two-word term names a short document that sets out an issue, the options and a recommendation for a senior decision-maker?
What one-word term names the person who guides a group discussion towards its aims without taking sides?
An agency invited 180 residents to a consultation meeting and 135 attended. What percentage attended?
What term names statements such as 'I am concerned when reports arrive late', which express a view without blaming the other person?
What one-word term names the ability to understand and share how another person feels?
What one-word term names a neutral person who helps two parties in conflict to reach their own agreement?
What term names the structured method in which members write ideas silently, share them in turn and then rank them?
What two-word term names a review of how well an organisation communicates, covering its channels, messages and the views of staff and users?

essays.stem: A ministry is introducing a complex new pension rule that affects serving staff, the staff unions and retired officers. Analyse their communication needs and plan a communication strategy.
essays.modelAnswer: Serving staff need to know how the rule affects their own future pension, what choices they must make and by when. Many will be anxious and may not understand pension terms. The unions have high power and high interest; they will want early, detailed information and a chance to raise concerns on their members' behalf. Retired officers mainly need reassurance about whether their current pensions change; many are older, some have limited internet access and some may have hearing or sight difficulties. The strategy would start with confidential briefings for the unions before any public announcement, so they are not surprised and can help explain the rule. Staff would then hear at the same time through unit meetings led by trained managers, a plain-language summary with worked examples, a set of frequently asked questions and a help line. Retirees would receive a short letter in large print stating clearly what changes and what does not, with a phone number and sessions in parish offices. Key messages would be agreed and all front-line staff briefed. Questions would be logged, and the strategy reviewed after a month.
markingPoints: Analyses staff needs and concerns
Analyses union power and interest
Analyses retirees' needs, including access
Sequenced plan with suitable channels for each group
Consistent key messages, support and review

essays.stem: Describe how you would plan and facilitate a public consultation meeting in a rural St Elizabeth community about a proposed waste disposal site.
essays.modelAnswer: I would plan with the project team to agree the purpose: to explain the proposal, hear residents' concerns and record ideas, making clear what is still open to change. I would choose a familiar, accessible venue, such as a community centre, at a time when working people can attend, and advertise through churches, schools, community groups, radio and notices. I would prepare simple maps, a plain-language summary and a technical officer to answer questions. At the meeting, I would welcome people, explain the purpose and agenda, and agree ground rules, such as one person speaking at a time and respect for all views. After a short presentation, I would invite questions, use small groups so quieter people can speak, and keep a list of issues outside the meeting's scope. I would stay neutral, manage strong emotions calmly and stop anyone dominating. A note-taker would record the main points without naming individuals unless they agree. At the end, I would summarise what was heard, explain the next steps and when people will hear back, and later publish a summary report.
markingPoints: Clear purpose and what is open to change
Accessible venue, timing and wide publicity
Opening with agenda and ground rules
Techniques for participation and handling emotion and dominance, staying neutral
Recording, summarising, next steps and feedback

essays.stem: Explain how an officer should handle a difficult conversation with an angry and distressed member of the public at a service counter.
essays.modelAnswer: The officer should first stay calm and keep a steady, polite tone, because anger is usually aimed at the situation rather than at her personally. She should move the conversation to a quieter area if possible, both for privacy and to reduce tension, while keeping her own safety in mind. She should let the person speak without interrupting, use active listening by nodding and paraphrasing, for example 'So you have been waiting three weeks for your payment', and acknowledge the person's feelings without arguing. Once the person feels heard, she should ask open questions to find out the facts and check the records. She should explain clearly what she can and cannot do, avoid jargon and never make promises she cannot keep. Where possible, she should offer a practical next step, such as escalating the case, with a time when the person will hear back. If the person becomes threatening, she should follow the safety procedure and call for help. Afterwards, she should record the conversation and any action promised, and follow up on time.
markingPoints: Stays calm and considers privacy and safety
Active listening and acknowledging feelings
Finds the facts with open questions
Explains clearly and honestly, offers next steps
Follows the safety procedure if needed; records and follows up

essays.stem: Two sections of a public agency are in conflict over shared vehicles, and their heads have stopped speaking to each other. Describe how you, as their manager, would use communication to resolve the conflict.
essays.modelAnswer: I would meet each section head separately first, in private, to hear their view, using open questions and active listening without taking sides. I would try to understand their underlying needs, for example one section needs vehicles early each morning for inspections, while the other needs them for long trips to rural parishes. I would then bring them together in a neutral setting, explain that the purpose is to find a workable solution, and agree ground rules, such as no interrupting and focusing on the problem rather than on each other. I would ask each to explain their needs, encourage them to use 'I' statements, and summarise what I heard to show both have been understood. Together we would look at the facts, such as vehicle use records, and generate options, such as a shared booking system, fixed time slots or pooling vehicles with another unit. We would agree a solution, record it in writing with who does what, and set a date to review it. I would keep an eye on their working relationship and recognise improvements.
markingPoints: Separate private meetings, listening without taking sides
Identifies underlying needs rather than positions
Joint meeting with purpose and ground rules
Uses facts and generates options together
Written agreement, review and follow-up

essays.stem: Compare face-to-face meetings, written circulars, the intranet and email, and video conferencing as ways to communicate a complex and sensitive change across a large public body, and recommend a combination.
essays.modelAnswer: Face-to-face meetings allow two-way discussion, questions and the reading of reactions, which matter when people are worried. They build trust but take time to organise across many offices, and the message may vary between presenters. Written circulars give an official, consistent record that staff can refer back to, but they are one-way, can be long and are often misunderstood without explanation. The intranet and email reach everyone quickly and cheaply and can hold detailed information and frequently asked questions, but they are easy to ignore, may not reach staff without computers, and are poor for emotional topics. Video conferencing can reach staff in distant parishes at the same time, allowing a senior leader to speak directly and take questions, but it depends on good connections, and some staff will not speak up online. I recommend a combination: a live video address by the head of the organisation to all staff at the same time, followed the same day by face-to-face meetings in each unit led by briefed managers using the same key messages, a written summary and FAQs on the intranet and by email, and a named contact for questions.
markingPoints: Face-to-face: strengths and limits
Written circulars: strengths and limits
Intranet and email: strengths and limits
Video conferencing: strengths and limits
Justified combination with consistent key messages

essays.stem: Explain how a public body should adapt its communication for people with low literacy, people with disabilities, people from other cultures and older people.
essays.modelAnswer: For people with low literacy, the body should use plain language, short sentences and pictures or diagrams, explain processes face to face or by phone, and check understanding by asking them to say back the main points, without making them feel ashamed. For people with disabilities, it should provide information in accessible formats, such as large print, audio and documents that work with screen readers, and arrange qualified sign language interpreters for Deaf people. Venues should be accessible, and staff should speak directly to the person, not to a companion. For people from other cultures or whose first language is not English, staff should avoid slang and idioms, speak clearly, allow time and use qualified interpreters for important matters rather than relying on family members. They should be aware that customs around eye contact, directness and formality differ. For older people, the body should keep paper and phone options alongside online services, use clear print and good lighting, and allow more time. In all cases, staff should ask people how they prefer to receive information and treat everyone with respect.
markingPoints: Low literacy: plain language, visuals, checking understanding
Disabilities: accessible formats, interpreters and venues
Other cultures and languages: clear speech, interpreters, awareness of customs
Older people: non-digital options and extra time
Asks preferences and shows respect

essays.stem: Describe how an officer should represent her work unit on an inter-agency task force on hurricane preparedness, from preparing for the first meeting to reporting back.
essays.modelAnswer: Before the first meeting, she should read the task force's terms of reference and agenda, and research the other agencies' roles. She should meet her manager to agree the unit's position on the main issues, the resources it can offer and the limits of what she may agree without referring back. She should prepare a short summary of her unit's role, its capacity and any concerns, with key facts. At the meeting, she should introduce her unit clearly, listen carefully to the other agencies and look for links and overlaps. She should present her unit's position confidently and politely, with evidence, while staying open to joint solutions. Where she is asked to commit staff or money beyond her authority, she should say she will refer it back and reply by an agreed date. She should build working relationships by being reliable and respectful, and note who is responsible for what. After the meeting, she should report promptly to her manager and unit in writing, giving the decisions made, actions her unit must take, deadlines and any issues needing a decision, and then follow through on her commitments.
markingPoints: Researches the task force and other agencies
Agrees position and authority limits with her manager
Presents clearly and listens for joint solutions
Refers commitments beyond her authority
Reports back promptly and follows through

essays.stem: Describe how you would prepare a briefing note on a complex issue for a Permanent Secretary, and how you would adapt the same content for a public information leaflet.
essays.modelAnswer: For the briefing note, I would first confirm what the Permanent Secretary needs to decide and by when. I would gather and check the facts, figures and legal or policy points, and consult the units affected. I would keep the note to about two pages, with a clear title and these parts: the purpose, stating the decision required; a short background; the key issues, with evidence; the options, each with its benefits, risks and costs; a clear recommendation with reasons; and the next steps. I would use a formal but plain style, short paragraphs and headings, and attach detailed data as an annex. I would mark it with the correct security level and have my manager check it. For the public leaflet, I would start from what members of the public need to know and do, not from the decision process. I would remove internal options, sensitive information and jargon, and use everyday words, short sentences, a friendly tone and simple headings such as 'What is changing' and 'What you need to do'. I would add examples, pictures and contact details, test it on a few readers, and provide accessible formats.
markingPoints: Confirms the decision needed and gathers checked facts
Clear briefing note structure with options and recommendation
Formal plain style, length and security marking
Leaflet focuses on what readers need to know and do, without sensitive detail
Plain language, examples, testing and accessible formats

essays.stem: A health department has run a three-month communication campaign to encourage residents to remove mosquito breeding sites. Explain how it should evaluate whether the campaign worked.
essays.modelAnswer: The department should begin with the campaign's objectives, which should be measurable, such as increasing the share of residents who can name three breeding sites and the share who check their yards weekly. It should compare results with baseline data collected before the campaign. First, it should measure reach: how many people saw or heard the messages, using radio airtime, social media views, leaflets delivered and attendance at community meetings. Second, it should measure understanding and attitudes, through a short survey of a random sample of residents in target communities, asking what they know and believe. Third, it should measure behaviour, for example through inspectors' checks of a sample of yards, comparing the number of breeding sites found with earlier inspections. It could also look at health data on dengue cases, while recognising that weather and other factors affect these figures. Focus groups would help explain why some messages worked and others did not. The department should then report the results, including limitations, and use the lessons to improve the next campaign, such as changing channels for groups that were not reached.
markingPoints: Starts from measurable objectives and a baseline
Measures reach
Measures understanding through a sample survey
Measures behaviour and outcomes, noting other factors
Uses qualitative methods, reports limits and applies lessons

essays.stem: Justify why a public body needs a deliberate communication strategy before announcing a contentious decision, such as the closure of a rural police station, and explain the risks of poor communication.
essays.modelAnswer: A contentious decision affects people's safety, services and feelings, so how it is communicated can matter as much as the decision itself. A deliberate strategy makes the body think in advance about who is affected, what each group needs to know, what they will worry about, and in what order they should hear. It ensures that staff and community leaders are told before the media, that every spokesperson gives the same accurate key messages, and that people are told the reasons, the alternatives being provided and how to raise concerns. It also prepares the body to listen and respond, which builds trust even when people disagree. Without a strategy, the risks are serious. Residents may first hear through rumour or social media, which creates fear and anger and spreads false information. Staff may feel betrayed and give mixed messages. Political and media criticism may grow, damaging trust in the organisation and making it harder to carry out future decisions. Vulnerable people may not learn about the replacement services. A planned strategy therefore protects the public, the staff and the organisation's reputation.
markingPoints: Explains why communication matters for contentious decisions
Strategy covers audiences, needs, sequence and key messages
Strategy includes reasons, alternatives and listening
Identifies risks of rumour, mixed messages and loss of trust
Considers vulnerable groups and reaches a justified conclusion

practical1.title: Plan a communication strategy for a contentious public decision
practical1.brief: The assessor gives your group a case pack for a made-up public body that must announce a contentious decision (for example a parish municipal corporation moving a popular market, a ministry merging two rural clinics, or an agency replacing counter services with an online system). The pack describes the decision, the people affected and some early reactions. As a group, produce: a stakeholder map on a power-interest grid; an audience analysis table showing each group's needs, concerns, preferred channels and any access needs; three to five key messages; a communication plan in a spreadsheet or table showing who is told what, by whom, through which channel and when, in the right order; and a one-page plain-language public notice with a short list of frequently asked questions. Give each member a named role: strategy lead (keeps time and writes the key messages), stakeholder analyst (builds the grid), audience analyst (builds the analysis table), planner (builds the communication plan) and public writer (writes the notice and FAQs). In a group of four, the strategy lead also writes the FAQs. Present the strategy to the assessor in ten minutes, with every member speaking. Photograph or screenshot each stage.
materials: Flipchart paper, sticky notes and markers
Computers with word-processing and spreadsheet or presentation software
photos: The power-interest grid on the flipchart
The communication plan showing the order of contact
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Identified all the main stakeholder groups and placed them sensibly on the grid
Audience analysis shows real needs, concerns and access needs
Key messages are accurate, consistent and plain
Plan puts the right people first and uses suitable channels
Public notice is clear, respectful and easy to read
Spoke clearly in the presentation and answered questions
safety: Use only the made-up case and invented names
Keep the case pack confidential to the group and the assessor
Discuss affected groups respectfully, without stereotypes
Share the workload fairly and take short screen breaks

practical2.title: Facilitate a stakeholder consultation and handle a difficult conversation
practical2.brief: The assessor gives your group a scenario for a made-up public consultation (for example on a new bus route, a market redevelopment or new opening hours at a public office) and role cards for participants with different views, including one who tends to dominate and one who is upset. In part one, the group plans and runs a 30-minute role-played consultation meeting with members of another group as participants: prepare an agenda and ground rules, open the meeting, manage the discussion, keep a list of off-agenda issues, and close with a summary and next steps. In part two, each pair in the group role-plays a 10-minute difficult conversation from the scenario (for example telling a vendor that a request has been refused, or calming an upset resident), swapping roles so that each member leads once. Produce: the agenda and ground rules on a flipchart; the meeting notes; a one-page summary report of what was heard; and a completed observer sheet for each difficult conversation. Give each member a named role: lead facilitator, co-facilitator (manages time and the off-agenda list), note-taker, observer (completes the observer sheets) and report writer. In a group of four, the note-taker also writes the report. Photograph each stage.
materials: Scenario and role cards from the assessor
Flipchart paper, markers and sticky notes
A meeting room set for 8 to 10 people, and computers for the report
photos: The agenda and ground rules on the flipchart
The meeting notes and summary report
A difficult conversation role play in progress
checklist: Took a named role and completed their part of the evidence
Opened the meeting with a clear purpose, agenda and ground rules
Managed the dominant participant politely and drew in quieter ones
Stayed neutral and summarised views fairly
In the difficult conversation, listened actively, stayed calm and explained clearly
Closed with clear next steps and recorded them accurately
safety: Role plays use made-up characters only; no one plays themselves or a real person
Anyone may pause a role play if it becomes uncomfortable
Keep notes about participants confidential to the group and the assessor
Speak respectfully, take short breaks and share the work fairly
